The upper end of the bridge is connected through a 100 Ω resistor to an op-amp-related node, and the lower end of the bridge is connected through another 100 Ω resistor to the op-amp inverting input/sensing node; this sensing node is also connected to ground through a 50 Ω resistor. The non-inverting terminal of the op-amp gives a 1 V reference, and the problem states that the op-amp is ideal. Reasoning: The ideal op-amp makes the voltage of the inverting input/sensing node equal to the non-inverting terminal reference voltage, namely 1 V. Therefore the current through the 50 Ω resistor is 1/50 = 0.02 A = 20 mA. Since the op-amp input current is zero, this current also flows through the lower 100 Ω, the bridge equivalent resistance, and the upper 100 Ω. Looking from the upper end to the lower end of the bridge, the resistance sum of each branch is 250(1+δ)+250(1−δ)=500 Ω; the two branches are in parallel, so the equivalent resistance is 250 Ω. The bridge excitation voltage is 20 mA × 250 Ω = 5 V. For this full bridge in the figure whose opposite bridge arms vary by ±δ, and with the right end of V0 positive, the output V0 = δ × 5 V. Substituting δ=0.05, V0 = 0.05 × 5 V = 0.25 V = 250 mV.

method.method_draft: First use the ideal op-amp condition: the node above the 50 Ω resistor is held at 1 V, so the current through the 50 Ω resistor is 20 mA. With no current entering the op-amp input, 20 mA must come through the lower 100 Ω resistor and through the bridge. The bridge branch sums are both 500 Ω in parallel, so the voltage across the bridge top-to-bottom is again 20 mA × 250 Ω = 5 V. Now avoid the bridge shortcut formula and compute the midpoint voltages directly. On the left branch, the midpoint voltage above the bottom bridge node is 5·[250(1−δ)/(250(1+δ)+250(1−δ))]=5(1−δ)/2. On the right branch it is 5·[250(1+δ)/(250(1−δ)+250(1+δ))]=5(1+δ)/2. Therefore V0=Vright−Vleft=5δ=0.25 V=250 mV for δ=0.05.

raw_record.final_cot: Image description: In the circuit there is a bridge network composed of four resistors; the upper-left and lower-right resistors are labeled 250(1+δ) Ω, and the upper-right and lower-left resistors are labeled 250(1−δ) Ω; V0 is labeled between the left and right midpoints of the bridge, with the right end positive and the left end negative. The upper end of the bridge is connected through a 100 Ω resistor to an op-amp-related node, and the lower end of the bridge is connected through another 100 Ω resistor to the op-amp inverting input/sensing node; this sensing node is also connected to ground through a 50 Ω resistor. The non-inverting terminal of the op-amp gives a 1 V reference, and the problem states that the op-amp is ideal. Reasoning: The ideal op-amp makes the voltage of the inverting input/sensing node equal to the non-inverting terminal reference voltage, namely 1 V. Therefore the current through the 50 Ω resistor is 1/50 = 0.02 A = 20 mA. Since the op-amp input current is zero, this current also flows through the lower 100 Ω, the bridge equivalent resistance, and the upper 100 Ω. Looking from the upper end to the lower end of the bridge, the resistance sum of each branch is 250(1+δ)+250(1−δ)=500 Ω; the two branches are in parallel, so the equivalent resistance is 250 Ω. The bridge excitation voltage is 20 mA × 250 Ω = 5 V. For this full bridge in the figure whose opposite bridge arms vary by ±δ, and with the right end of V0 positive, the output V0 = δ × 5 V. Substituting δ=0.05, V0 = 0.05 × 5 V = 0.25 V = 250 mV.
